commit.message:
fix: [security] Mass assignment fix sweep

ServersController: add() saved $this->request->data directly with no
fieldList and no id strip, so an injected Server[id] turned the create
into a covert UPDATE of an arbitrary server row (milestone Servers of the
mass-assignment audit).
- add() is REST-reachable (/servers/add.json); CSRF field-hashing does not
  cover the REST path, so a site-admin key could repoint another server's
  sync url/authkey/push-pull rules while it is logged as an "add".
- Strip the client-supplied id before save() (this action only ever
  creates). edit() already pins id to the route + uses a fieldList that
  excludes org_id; import()/createSync() build fresh whitelisted arrays
  (no id); other writes act on DB-loaded records - all SAFE.
- Live-proven before/after: strip disabled -> POST id=2 overwrote server 2's
  url/authkey; strip enabled -> new row created, server 2 untouched.
- as reported by Jeroen Pinoy

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
fix: [security] Mass assignment fix sweep

TaxonomiesController/Taxonomy::import allowed an injected nested id to
redirect and re-own the deep saveAssociated() (milestone Taxonomies of
the mass-assignment audit).

- Taxonomy::__updateVocab() (the import/update capture sink) builds a
  fresh top-level Taxonomy array (no id), but copied the request-supplied
  predicate and entry arrays verbatim into saveAssociated(['deep'=>true]).
  TaxonomyPredicate/TaxonomyEntry have no id strip and no FK forcing, so a
  crafted predicate/entry `id` turned the deep INSERT into an UPDATE that
  re-parented and overwrote a predicate/entry owned by another taxonomy.
- Live-proven: importing a NEW namespace whose predicate carried another
  taxonomy's predicate id silently moved that predicate (and its value)
  into the attacker taxonomy, stripping it from the victim taxonomy, all
  logged merely as "imported <attacker>". Reachable via /taxonomies/import
  (site-admin only -> adversarial-site-admin covert-redirection lens).
- Fixed by unset()-ing `id` on each nested predicate and entry before the
  save; imports only ever create fresh rows. Live before/after proven
  (post-fix the injected ids are ignored, fresh rows inserted, victim
  taxonomy intact).
- as reported by Jeroen Pinoy

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
fix: [security] Mass assignment fix sweep

ShadowAttributesController: two scope-FK mass-assignment issues on the proposal
create paths (id-hijack itself was already closed; edit() was hardened earlier in
9341690e9). Both let a body-supplied foreign key diverge from the route the ACL
validated.

- add(): the action only ever proposes NEW attributes (edit-proposals go through
  edit()), yet old_id and uuid were caller-controlled. A REST caller could submit
  old_id!=0 plus an arbitrary uuid; on acceptance ShadowAttribute::acceptProposal()
  takes the old_id!=0 branch, finds the live attribute by that uuid and overwrites
  (or, with proposal_to_delete, deletes) it — retargeting an accepted proposal onto
  an attribute it was never meant to touch. Pin old_id to 0 so every add() proposal
  is unambiguously a new-attribute proposal.
- add_attachment(): event_id was read from the request body (Attribute[event_id])
  for both the malware-sample and plain-attachment proposals, while the ACL
  validated the route event and event_uuid/event_org_id were taken from it. A caller
  could land a proposal on an event they were never authorised against. Pin event_id
  to the route-validated event (matching add(), which already does this).

Live-verified before/after on the dev instance: pre-fix an injected old_id=99999
was stored verbatim and an add_attachment posted to route event X with body
event_id=Y landed on Y; post-fix old_id is forced to 0 and the attachment lands on X.

Milestone ShadowAttributesController of the mass-assignment audit.
- as reported by Jeroen Pinoy

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
fix: [preventative] pre-empting a future possible mass assignment vulnerability

Mass-assignment audit Tier B #6 — TemplatesController. Two sink-level
hardenings. NOT exploitable on current code (see below), hence the
preventative tag rather than the [security] sweep title: the fixes
close the sinks so they stay safe regardless of the fragile gate that
currently protects them.

add(): calls Template->create()+save() on raw request->data while
forcing org to the caller's org, but never strips id. CakePHP create()
does not strip a supplied primary key, so an injected Template[id] turns
the INSERT into a covert UPDATE that overwrites another org's template
and re-owns it via the forced org (the Servers 00b2e3dae / TagCollections
c80a3533b pattern). perm_template-reachable. Fixed by unset id before
create() (edit() already pins id to the route @53).

submitEventPopulation(): saves the reviewed attributes straight from
json_decode(request->data['Template']['attributes']) via a direct
MispAttribute->save with no event_id pin and no id strip. This bypasses
captureAttribute, and only the ROUTE event_id was ACL-checked, so a body
event_id would inject attributes onto an arbitrary event and a body id
would covertly UPDATE an arbitrary attribute (the add_threatconnect
58f637aaa / Events freetext bc182d55d class). perm_add-reachable. Fixed
by pinning event_id to the route-authorised event and unsetting id in
the save loop (checkTemplateAttributes already forces event_id=route in
the review step, so legit flows are unaffected).

Why preventative, not [security]: both POST actions are currently
unreachable via REST — the controller's beforeFilter (marked
"// TODO REMOVE") clobbers parent::beforeFilter()'s REST unlockedActions
back to a hardcoded list excluding add/edit/submitEventPopulation, so
REST POSTs are black-holed (verified: /templates/add.json black-holed
while /events/add.json succeeded). On the web path, SecurityComponent
salt-based field-hashing blocks the injection: verified live as a lesser
perm_template user with the fix reverted — a faithful legit add returned
302 and created a row, while the identical request plus an injected
Template[id]=1 was black-holed (HTTP 400) and template 1 was untouched.
submitEventPopulation's tamper target (the attributes field) is a hidden
input, so its value is locked the same way. If a future change removes
the "// TODO REMOVE" beforeFilter clobber as instructed, these actions
become REST-reachable (SecurityComponent off for REST) and both holes
would open — these fixes pre-empt exactly that.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
fix: [security] Mass assignment fix sweep

Mass-assignment audit Tier B #7 — TemplateElementsController. LIVE,
REST-reachable, perm_template (lesser-user) id-redirection in the nested
sub-element save of add() and addV2().

Both add($type,$id) and addV2($id) create a fresh base TemplateElement
(template_id forced to the route-authorised template) and then save the
type-specific sub-model (TemplateElementAttribute / TemplateElementText /
TemplateElementFile) straight from $this->request->data. They force the
sub-model's template_element_id to the new base element but never strip
id; create() before save() does NOT strip a supplied primary key, and the
sub-models have no beforeSave/id-guard. So an injected
TemplateElement<Type>[id] turns the INSERT into a covert UPDATE that
re-parents (via the forced template_element_id) and overwrites an
arbitrary element row owned by another org's template.

Unlike TemplatesController this controller has NO beforeFilter clobber of
the REST unlockedActions, so parent::beforeFilter() leaves the action
REST-unlocked and SecurityComponent field-hashing does not apply on the
REST path — the hole is live, not preventative.

Fixed by unsetting the sub-model id before create()+save() in both add()
and addV2() (edit()/editV2() already pin it to the loaded row).

Verified live as lesser user 184 (org 156, perm_template, NOT site-admin)
via REST POST /template_elements/add/attribute/<own-template-id> with an
injected TemplateElementAttribute[id]=1: pre-fix the victim attribute
(template 1, org "MISP", "From address") was overwritten and re-parented
onto the attacker's template (template_element_id moved, name/to_ids
overwritten); post-fix the same request left the victim untouched and
inserted a fresh row under the attacker's own template. DB restored,
test artifacts cleaned.

Other actions SAFE: edit()/editV2() pin sub-model id + template_element_id
to the loaded record (no redirection); delete() loads by route id and
deletes the loaded sub-model/base ids; deleteSelection checkModifyCallback
returns perm_site_admin (SAFE gate, not DPT-1); index/templateElementAddChoices
read-only.

Out of mass-assignment scope, flagged for the post-sweep follow-up
(PRD §12 DPT-5): edit($type,$id) authorises checkAuthorisation($id, ...)
where $id is the template ELEMENT id, but checkAuthorisation expects a
TEMPLATE id (wrong-entity authz, the DPT-3 class). editV2 does it right
(authorises the loaded element's parent template). Narrowly exploitable
(needs a coincidentally-id'd owned template) and the save id is pinned to
the loaded record, so it is broken-access-control, not mass-assignment;
left for the deferred ACL sub-project.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
fix: [preventative] pre-empting a future possible mass assignment vulnerability

WorkflowsController mass-assignment audit (Tier B #19) — SAFE, defence-in-depth
hardening of the one footgun.

Workflow::addWorkflow() calls create() then save() with a fieldList that omits
`id`. A fieldList limits which columns are written, NOT the INSERT-vs-UPDATE
decision: CakePHP Model::set() seeds $this->id from a client-supplied
Workflow[id], so an injected id turns the intended INSERT into a covert UPDATE
of an arbitrary workflow row (overwriting name/description/data/trigger_id/uuid/
debug_enabled). REST-reachable (no unlockedActions clobber in beforeFilter).

Not currently exploitable: workflows is global config (no org/user ownership FK,
no secrets) and add/edit share the same site-admin-only ACL with no per-row
scope, so the redirect only reaches rows the actor can already overwrite via
edit($id) — identical to the Regexp admin_add footgun. Hardened anyway, per
user request, with an id-strip covering both the wrapped (add) and flat (editor)
caller shapes; protects all future callers of the model helper.

edit() is already doubly id-safe (inverse-merge from the route-loaded record in
__applyDataFromSavedWorkflow ignoring id/uuid, then editWorkflow re-pins id via
fetchWorkflow). All other write actions (toggleModule/massToggleField -> redis,
toggleDebug -> loaded record, executeWorkflow/moduleStatelessExecution -> runtime
only, delete -> CRUD route id) reach no request-data row save.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
fix: [security] Mass assignment fix sweep

AttributesController: add_threatconnect checked __canModifyEvent() on the
*route* event ($eventId) but built every imported attribute's event_id (and the
post-import "unpublish" saveField) from the attacker-controlled request body
field Attribute[event_id]. A user able to modify any one event could therefore
inject ThreatConnect-CSV attributes into — and unpublish — an arbitrary event
they have no rights to (mass-assignment scope injection via event_id; the model
save path performs no event-ownership check). Pin all three sinks to the
ACL-validated route $eventId; the legitimate UI form already posts the same id,
so behaviour is unchanged for normal use.

Live-verified before/after on the dev instance: pre-fix, an attribute posted to
route event X with body event_id=Y landed in Y and flipped Y's published flag
1->0; post-fix the same request lands in X and leaves Y untouched.

Milestone AttributesController of the mass-assignment audit.

commit.message:
fix: [security] Mass assignment fix sweep

GalaxyClusterRelations: edit() and add() let a perm_galaxy_editor cross a
privilege/scope boundary via body-supplied scope FKs (milestone
GalaxyClusterRelations of the mass-assignment audit).

- edit(): authorised and saved the source cluster from the body
  galaxy_cluster_uuid, while the relation itself was only loaded with VIEW
  scope (fetchRelations). A user who could merely VIEW a relation on another
  org's cluster could re-parent it onto a cluster they own (supply their own
  cluster's uuid to pass the edit check), silently removing the relation from
  the victim cluster - a cross-cluster relation hijack. Pinned
  galaxy_cluster_uuid to the stored relation's source so both the auth check
  and the saved galaxy_cluster_id derive from the relation's real owner,
  matching delete() which already authorises against the stored source uuid.
  Live before/after proven (org-316 editor moved org-1's relation; after fix
  the edit is rejected and the row is untouched; legit owner edit still works).
- add(): distribution 4 (sharing group) did not validate SG access, letting a
  galaxy editor scope a relation to a sharing group they cannot access
  (editRelation() already enforces this via checkIfAuthorised). Added the same
  checkIfAuthorised gate on the add path. Live-proven (SG the user has no
  access to is now rejected).
- Guarded the now-reachable un-owned-source auth-failure path so the rejection
  returns a clean error instead of dereferencing a missing GalaxyCluster key.
- as reported by Jeroen Pinoy

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: [security] Mass assignment fix sweep

CRUDComponent::edit() central id-pin (Milestone 0 of the controller
mass-assignment audit).

  including a payload-supplied primary key, so an injected id redirected the

commit.message:
fix: [security] Mass assignment fix sweep

CollectionsController::edit() — sharing-group authorisation parity gap.

The distribution=4 sharing-group access check (checkIfCanBeUsed) only ran
when 'distribution' was present in the request body. CRUDComponent::edit()
retains the stored value for any field the request omits and applies no
fields whitelist here, so a perm_modify user editing their own collection
could retarget an existing distribution=4 collection onto a sharing group
they are NOT authorised to use simply by omitting 'distribution' (it stays
4 from the stored record) while mass-assigning sharing_group_id. The add
path correctly gates the SG on create; this restores parity on edit (same
class as the EventReports editReport fix ab9619dfa).

Fix: validate the EFFECTIVE distribution (body value if present, else the
stored value) and run checkIfCanBeUsed against the effective sharing group
whenever the effective distribution is 4 and the request actually changes
the distribution or the sharing group. An untouched SG on an unrelated edit
is left as-is so a legitimate owner can still edit other fields without the
check firing on a now-unauthorised stale SG. REST-reachable, so CSRF
field-hashing is irrelevant.

their collection to SG 19 pre-fix; post-fix the same request is rejected
with "Invalid Sharing Group or not authorised." and the stored SG is
preserved; legit name-only / authorised-SG / distribution-downgrade edits
still succeed.

commit.message:
fix: [security] Mass assignment fix sweep

BookmarksController::edit allowed mass-assignment of the Bookmark.user_id
ownership FK. The action has no `fields` whitelist, so CRUDComponent::edit
merges every posted field onto the loaded record; Bookmark::beforeValidate
force-pins user_id only on the create branch (empty id), and M0 re-pins
only id. An injected Bookmark[user_id] therefore re-owned the bookmark to
an arbitrary victim user.

Impact: bookmarks ACL is ['*'] (any authenticated user, incl. read-only)
and the controller has no beforeFilter unlockedActions clobber, so the
edit sink is REST-reachable with the Security component off. A low-priv
user could create their own bookmark (add force-pins user_id), then edit

re-owned row surfaces in the victim's global navigation menu

matches on user_id and ignores org_id) across orgs -> stored phishing /
malicious-link injection. Same add/edit parity class as the

(the form's own fields), excluding the user_id/org_id ownership FKs; id is
covered by the central CRUD edit id-pin, exposed_to_org/org_id remain
gated by beforeValidate. Live before/after proven: pre-fix an injected

preserved) while name/url still update.

commit.message:
fix: [security] Mass assignment fix sweep

TagCollectionsController::addWithTags() — id-redirection in a create-only action.

addWithTags() builds the save array straight from request->data, forces
org_id/user_id to the current user, then calls TagCollection->saveAssociated()
without ever stripping the primary key. CakePHP treats an id present in the save
data as an UPDATE target, so a supplied TagCollection[id] turned the insert into
a covert UPDATE of an arbitrary tag collection — and because org_id/user_id are
force-pinned to the attacker, that row was simultaneously re-owned to them
(overwrite + steal). Reachable by a non-site-admin perm_tag_editor user (ACL:
perm_tag_editor + theming_enabled), so the lesser-user model applies; REST-
reachable, so CSRF field-hashing does not help.

always inserts a new row, mirroring TagCollection::import() (which already strips
id + forces ownership) and the edit/editWithTags paths (which pin id to the
authorised record).

{"TagCollection":{"id":1,...}} to addWithTags — pre-fix org-1's collection 1 was
overwritten and re-owned to org-531; post-fix collection 1 is untouched and a new
row is inserted instead. Legitimate creation still works.

ownership), import (model strips id + forces ownership, dedups by uuid), edit /

commit.message:
fix(release): gate draft release attachments on web download endpoints (#38318) (#38325)

Backport #38318 by @bircni

Draft-release access control was enforced only on the API release
endpoints (`/api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases/...`) but not on the
UUID-based web attachment endpoints (`/attachments/{uuid}`,
`/{owner}/{repo}/attachments/{uuid}`,
`/{owner}/{repo}/releases/attachments/{uuid}`).

Anyone who obtained an attachment UUID — including unauthenticated
callers — could download files belonging to a hidden draft release,
since `ServeAttachment` only checked repo-level read permission and
never the release's draft state.

This extends `ServeAttachment` to require write access to releases when
the attachment belongs to a draft release, mirroring the existing
API-side `canAccessReleaseDraft` gate. A regression test is included.

Co-authored-by: bircni <bircni@icloud.com>

+func TestNewProxyFunc(t *testing.T) {
+	fixedProxy, err := url.Parse("http://proxy.example:3128")
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	// simulate a configured proxy that would be used for every request
+	base := func(*http.Request) (*url.URL, error) { return fixedProxy, nil }
+
+	newReq := func(rawURL string) *http.Request {
+		r, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, rawURL, nil)
+		require.NoError(t, err)
+		return r
+	}
+
+	t.Run("blocks non-allowed target on the proxy path", func(t *testing.T) {
+		pf := NewProxyFunc("test", ParseHostMatchList("test", "example.com"), nil, base)
+		_, err := pf(newReq("http://evil.example/"))
+		assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "can only call allowed HTTP servers")
+	})
+
+	t.Run("blocks link-local metadata even with external allow-list", func(t *testing.T) {
+		pf := NewProxyFunc("test", ParseHostMatchList("test", MatchBuiltinExternal), nil, base)
+		_, err := pf(newReq("http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"))
+		assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "can only call allowed HTTP servers")
+	})
+
+	t.Run("allows a listed target on the proxy path", func(t *testing.T) {
+		pf := NewProxyFunc("test", ParseHostMatchList("test", "example.com"), nil, base)
+		proxyURL, err := pf(newReq("http://example.com/avatar.png"))
+		assert.NoError(t, err)
+		assert.Equal(t, fixedProxy, proxyURL)
+	})
+
+	// a bare hostname must be resolved so an IP-based builtin can authorize it; without resolution the
+	// `loopback`/`external` builtins never match a DNS name and every proxied fetch would be refused.
+	t.Run("resolves a hostname so an IP builtin can allow it", func(t *testing.T) {
+		pf := NewProxyFunc("test", ParseHostMatchList("test", MatchBuiltinLoopback), nil, base)
+		proxyURL, err := pf(newReq("http://localhost/avatar.png"))
+		assert.NoError(t, err)
+		assert.Equal(t, fixedProxy, proxyURL)
+	})
+
+	t.Run("resolves a hostname so an external builtin refuses a loopback name", func(t *testing.T) {
+		pf := NewProxyFunc("test", ParseHostMatchList("test", MatchBuiltinExternal), nil, base)
+		_, err := pf(newReq("http://localhost/avatar.png"))
+		assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "can only call allowed HTTP servers")
+	})
+
+	// the block-list must also be enforced on the proxy path (migration keeps a block-list and often an
+	// empty allow-list); otherwise a proxy could reach a blocked target unchecked.
+	t.Run("enforces the block-list on the proxy path", func(t *testing.T) {
+		pf := NewProxyFunc("test", nil, ParseHostMatchList("test", MatchBuiltinLoopback), base)
+		_, err := pf(newReq("http://localhost/"))
+		assert.ErrorContains(t, err, "can not call blocked HTTP servers")
+	})
+
+	t.Run("no proxy configured leaves validation to the dialer", func(t *testing.T) {
+		noProxy := func(*http.Request) (*url.URL, error) { return nil, nil } //nolint:nilnil // mimics proxy.Proxy() selecting no proxy
+		pf := NewProxyFunc("test", ParseHostMatchList("test", MatchBuiltinExternal), nil, noProxy)
+		proxyURL, err := pf(newReq("http://169.254.169.254/"))
+		assert.NoError(t, err)
+		assert.Nil(t, proxyURL)
+	})
+}

commit.message:
Harden combined resource handler against forged resource IDs

Combined resource IDs are unauthenticated deflate+base64 of the resource
list, so a crafted ID could inflate without bound, grow the static cache
without bound, and select arbitrary inner resources at serve time.

- Cap unserializeURLSafe output at 64 KiB.
- Populate the info cache only from the render path (Builder.create); the
  serve path no longer caches reconstructed IDs.
- Serve a reconstructed ID only when every inner resource is a stylesheet
  or script, so a forged ID cannot reference Facelets or dynamic resources.

Ref GHSA-fp43-vj7g-pg92

commit.message:
Restrict session and view scoped push channels to their owning HTTP session

The web socket handshake accepted any client presenting a known channel ID,
so a leaked session or view scoped channel ID could be connected to from a
foreign or absent HTTP session. Bind those channels to the HTTP session that
registered them and refuse the handshake otherwise. Application scoped
channels stay unbound by design.

Also make the endpoint idle timeout and the maximum number of sessions per
channel operator-configurable, both defaulting to the current behavior:

- org.omnifaces.SOCKET_ENDPOINT_IDLE_TIMEOUT (default 0, i.e. no timeout)
- org.omnifaces.SOCKET_MAX_SESSIONS_PER_CHANNEL (default unbounded)

Ref GHSA-fp43-vj7g-pg92

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
